provenance.pipeline: satsuki v1 (v1.0.1 editorial re-edit: usage-note reshaping corpus-wide, lane discrimination for same-surface families, against prompts/style.md)

patterns.usage_note: Reports a conclusion resting on information that reached the speaker from outside, heard or read or inferred from circumstances not witnessed firsthand (試合は中止になったらしい). ようだ rests on evidence the speaker took in directly, and みたい is the colloquial form of that inference. It attaches straight to plain forms and to bare nouns, with no の or な. The suffix らしい in 男らしい is a different word.

examples.ruby: 隣[となり]のご主人[しゅじん]、来月[らいげつ]大阪[おおさか]に転勤[てんきん]するらしいです。
examples.english: Apparently the husband next door is being transferred to Osaka next month.

examples.ruby: 昨日[きのう]の試合[しあい]は大雨[おおあめ]で中止[ちゅうし]になったらしい。
examples.english: I hear yesterday's match got called off because of the downpour.

examples.ruby: あの峠[とうげ]の道[みち]は思[おも]った以上[いじょう]に険[けわ]しいらしい。
examples.english: That mountain-pass road is supposedly steeper than you'd expect.

patterns.usage_note: Draws an inference from what the speaker sees, hears, or feels, with the grounds usually stated in the same sentence: 顔が赤いから熱があるようだ, どうやら道を間違えたようだ. The sibling lane is likening, holding one thing against a standard of comparison (氷のようだ, 飛ぶように走る). After a noun it takes の and after a na-adjective な, where casual みたい attaches bare, and らしい puts the grounds in an outside source.

examples.ruby: 喉[のど]が痛[いた]いし体[からだ]も重[おも]い、風邪[かぜ]をひいたようだ。
examples.english: My throat hurts and my body feels heavy — it seems I've caught a cold.

examples.ruby: どうやら私[わたし]は道[みち]を一本[いっぽん]間違[まちが]えたようだ。
examples.english: It seems I took the wrong street.

examples.ruby: 改札[かいさつ]の前[まえ]に人[ひと]が集[あつ]まっている、電車[でんしゃ]が遅[おく]れているようです。
examples.english: People are bunched up in front of the ticket gates; it looks like the trains are running late.

patterns.usage_note: Draws a conclusion from the evidence in front of the speaker (時計が止まっているから電池が切れたみたい, まだ起きているみたい). The sibling lane is plain resemblance, one thing held up against a standard (真夏みたいに暑い). It attaches straight to a noun with no の (病気みたいだ) and stays conversational, with ようだ in formal writing. らしい usually relays what someone else reported, みたい the speaker's own impression.

examples.ruby: 二階[にかい]の住人[じゅうにん]、まだ起[お]きているみたいだね。
examples.english: Looks like the folks upstairs are still up.

examples.ruby: スープの味[あじ]が薄[うす]い、塩[しお]を入[い]れ忘[わす]れたみたい。
examples.english: The soup tastes thin — looks like I forgot the salt.

examples.ruby: 時計[とけい]の針[はり]が止[と]まっているから、電池[でんち]が切[き]れたみたい。
examples.english: The clock hands aren't moving, so it looks like the battery died.
